messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The event that changed everything for Marcus happened on a Tuesday evening in late autumn, two years ago. He had been driving home from his dental practice, tired after a long day of crown preps and root canals, when he stopped at a gas station off the interstate to fill up. He was parked, pumping gas, when a patrol car pulled in behind him. The officer stepped out and approached his car window without explanation. Marcus had barely rolled it down before the man’s hand shot through the gap, grabbing his collar, yanking him sideways. He was on the ground in seconds, knees in his back, the officer shouting something about a stolen vehicle—a mistake that would take three hours to sort out at the station, where they finally admitted the plates didn’t match. But by then the damage was done. Marcus’s ribs had been cracked, his jaw wrenched so badly he couldn’t open his mouth fully for weeks. And there was something else, something that stayed with him long after the bruises faded: the sound of the officer’s radio squawking static just before the first blow, and the sharp, grinding pain in his lower back as his body was twisted against the asphalt.

Now, two years later, Marcus cannot hear static without his chest tightening. He avoids watching television shows that feature police scanners, and he has stopped listening to talk radio altogether because the crackle of a bad signal sends him into a cold sweat. The memory of that night feels like it belongs to someone else—a stranger’s life, not his own. When he tries to recall it, he often finds himself thinking, *that didn’t happen to me*, even as the auditory flashbacks arrive unbidden: the squawk of the radio, the officer’s breathless commands, the metallic click of handcuffs. And then, without warning, a phantom ache will settle into his lower back, just above his left hip, the same spot where the pavement had ground into his spine. He has come to believe there is something fundamentally wrong with him, something that made this happen. He was just a dentist, a man in his late fifties, driving a sensible sedan—why would an officer target him if not because of something about his face, his skin, his presence? The injustice of it gnaws at him daily. Nothing was done. The officer was not disciplined. Marcus filed a complaint; it was dismissed. His life, he is certain, has been destroyed.

At work, Marcus has become a different man. He used to chat easily with patients, but now he finds himself scanning the waiting room before every appointment, checking who is sitting where, whether anyone has their hands in their pockets. He has started choosing his own seat in the break room with his back to the wall, facing the door. He avoids any conversation that might become stressful—a patient’s complaint about insurance, a hygienist’s question about scheduling—and he has begun to cancel on patients he does not know well, claiming illness. His partner, Linda, has noticed that he no longer wants to go to restaurants or grocery stores. He says it is because he is tired, but the truth is that every stranger who walks toward him on the sidewalk feels like a potential threat. He has stopped seeing his friends entirely; their invitations to dinner or a ballgame feel like demands he cannot meet without first scanning the parking lot for police cars.

Sleep has become a battleground. Marcus lies awake for hours, his mind replaying the sound of the radio, the pressure of the knee, the grinding pain. When he finally drifts off, he wakes in the small hours, heart pounding, convinced he heard a car door slam outside. He has begun checking the locks on the doors and windows three times before bed, and he insists on sleeping on the side of the bed farthest from the door. Linda has grown frustrated; she does not understand why he cannot just let it go.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a moment in his own office, three weeks ago. A new patient—a young man in his twenties, wearing a hooded sweatshirt—walked into the operatory, and Marcus felt his throat close. He could not speak. He stood frozen, staring at the man’s hands, until his assistant touched his arm and asked if he was alright. He excused himself, went to the bathroom, and vomited. That night, he told Linda he could not go on like this. He is afraid of what will happen if he does not change—afraid he will lose his practice, lose her, lose himself entirely. And yet, what he hopes for, more than anything, is to feel safe in his own skin again, to walk into a room without first calculating the exits.
